title: Mississauga father gunned down by police suffered from schizophrenia
article: A 49-year-old Mississauga man suffering from schizophrenia was killed by Toronto Police in a hail of bullets after driving recklessly and injuring an officer in the process, a coroner's jury has heard.

Wieslaw Duda was killed inside his vehicle in Toronto's Port Lands area in the early morning of April 19, 2010. During the police chase which was sparked when he refused to stop for police, Duda injured Toronto Const. Curtis Hibbert, 48, an accomplished Mississauga gymnast who represented Canada twice at the Olympics. He was the first Canadian gymnast to win a medal at the world championships, taking a silver in 1987.
More than 30 shots were fired by five officers after Duda accelerated his car past a police roadblock and hit Hibbert, who suffered minor injuries.

The coroner's inquest being held this week will examine of how Toronto police react to people experiencing a mental crisis. Duda, a father of two who separated from his wife, immigrated to Canada from Poland more than 15 years ago. Shortly after his death, one neighbour said Duda worked at a Mississauga factory but had gone on a medical disability leave.
Hours before the fatal shooting, Duda's family phoned Peel Regional Police concerned about his behaviour. It isn't yet known how the Peel force responded to the call.

The province's Special Investigations Unit, a provincial body that probes incidents in which civilians are injured or killed during interactions with police to determine whether officers will be charged, looked into Duda's death and ruled that lethal force was justified.
The SIU received a 9-1-1 call reporting that Duda was operating a motor vehicle "in an erratic manner, swerving all over the road."
Two officers were dispatched to investigate and other officers investigating a gas leak became involved in the chase when Duda whizzed by them.
"In addition to driving at a very high rate of speed during this pursuit, Mr. Duda ignored numerous red traffic signal lights," the SIU probe found.
The chase continued after Duda struck one of the police vehicles, but was later called off because of threats to public safety.
Other officers arrived at the intersection of Cherry and Commissioners Sts., exited their vehicles, and took up positions of cover with their guns drawn, the SIU said.

Just after 1:30 a.m. Duda's vehicle arrived and momentarily stopped just east of the intersection. Several officers, with pistols unholstered, shouted at Duda to show his hands and get out of the car.

Duda did not comply with the officers' commands and instead accelerated in their direction. As the officers scrambled to get out of the path of the vehicle, one of the officers - Hibbert - was struck by Duda's vehicle and was propelled onto the vehicle causing its windshield to shatter. He then rolled off.
At about the same instant that Duda's vehicle struck the officer, several officers discharged a total of 32 rounds from their pistols at Duda, and one officer discharged his shotgun twice at the man.
The gunfire ceased when Duda's vehicle collided with a police cruiser.
Several bullets fired by two officers struck Duda's torso and caused his death, the SIU found.

The inquest, expected to last a month, will hear from the officers involved, police training experts, a forensic pathologist and others to discuss questions surrounding actions taken by officers in the lead-up to Duda's death. Among the issues likely to arise is whether police could have employed less lethal force, such as a spike belt, to halt Duda's vehicle.
